candidate.blueprint_locator: Client Needs category 'Psychosocial Integrity' — nursing care that promotes and supports emotional, mental and social well-being; applied here to anxiety, coping, therapeutic communication, psychosocial assessment and referral during survivorship.
candidate.educational_objective: Respond to fear of cancer recurrence by validating the concern, assessing its functional and care impact, supporting recommended follow-up, and facilitating psychosocial help when anxiety becomes difficult to manage.

options.A: Acknowledge the fear, assess how much it is affecting daily function and follow-up care, encourage the client to keep the recommended follow-up plan, and offer psychosocial support or counseling if needed.
options.B: Tell the client there is no reason to worry because completing treatment guarantees that the cancer will not recur.
options.C: Support canceling the scan because avoiding cancer-related reminders is the best way to reduce fear of recurrence.
options.D: Explain that fear of recurrence is abnormal after treatment and by itself proves the client has a psychiatric disorder.

candidate.rationale: A is correct. NCI describes fear of cancer recurrence as a common survivorship concern and notes that follow-up scans and other medical tests can trigger substantial anxiety or 'scanxiety.' NCI advises survivors to tell the healthcare team about recurrence fears, maintain follow-up care, and seek counseling when fear becomes more than they can manage. Psychosocial assessment should consider how distress affects functioning and care. B is incorrect because treatment completion does not guarantee that recurrence is impossible. C reinforces avoidance of recommended follow-up rather than addressing the fear. D incorrectly pathologizes a common survivorship concern without assessing its severity or impact.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Fear of recurrence is common after treatment and may intensify around scans/follow-up; survivors should discuss it with the healthcare team, maintain follow-up care, and may need psychosocial support when fear interferes with coping or function.
